concepts.name: Formation Conditions for Tropical Cyclones (Genesis Criteria)
key_dimensions: Six necessary conditions: SST ≥26-27°C, Coriolis force (absent within 5° of equator), low vertical wind shear, pre-existing disturbance, warm deep ocean layer, and atmospheric instability
UPSC trap: Why cyclones do NOT form on the equator despite warmest SSTs — Coriolis force angle
Why South Atlantic and SE Pacific rarely see tropical cyclones despite warm SSTs — cold upwelling + high wind shear
Role of ITCZ and easterly waves as seedling disturbances

concepts.name: Structure of a Tropical Cyclone: Eye, Eye Wall, and Spiral Rainbands
key_dimensions: Eye characteristics: calm, warm, subsiding air, clear skies, lowest pressure — counterintuitive to exam takers
Eye wall: most violent winds, heaviest rainfall, tallest cumulonimbus towers — contrast with eye
Spiral rainbands: alternating zones of precipitation and clear air; outflow at upper levels
Eye wall replacement cycle: weakening then re-intensification — relevance to forecasting intensity

concepts.name: Energy Source and Warm Core vs. Cold Core Distinction
key_dimensions: Tropical cyclones: warm-core, derive energy from latent heat of condensation over warm oceans (CISK mechanism)
Temperate/extratropical cyclones: cold-core, derive energy from horizontal temperature gradients (baroclinic instability)
UPSC trap: Warm-core = tropical; Cold-core = temperate — used to distinguish in MCQs
Why tropical cyclones weaken over land or cold water — cutoff from moisture and heat source

concepts.name: Classification and Nomenclature of Tropical Cyclones Globally
key_dimensions: Regional naming: Hurricane (Atlantic/NE Pacific), Typhoon (NW Pacific), Cyclone (Indian Ocean/SW Pacific), Willy-Willy (Australia — now largely archaic)
Saffir-Simpson scale (1–5) for hurricanes vs. IMD's 7-tier classification for Indian Ocean cyclones
UPSC trap: Saffir-Simpson is based on wind speed only, NOT storm surge or rainfall
WMO Regional Specialized Meteorological Centres (RSMCs) — India's RSMC at New Delhi covers North Indian Ocean

concepts.name: Movement and Track of Tropical Cyclones
key_dimensions: General westward movement in tropics due to trade winds (easterlies), then poleward recurvature due to westerlies
Recurvature point: critical for landfall prediction — Bay of Bengal vs. Arabian Sea cyclone tracks
UPSC trap: Arabian Sea cyclones historically fewer and weaker than Bay of Bengal — reasons (cooler SST, drier air, higher wind shear) — but trend reversing with climate change
Role of subtropical ridge in steering cyclones; interaction with upper-level troughs triggering recurvature

concepts.name: Bay of Bengal vs. Arabian Sea Cyclone Asymmetry
key_dimensions: Bay of Bengal: ~80% of all North Indian Ocean cyclones — warm, enclosed, low salinity (freshwater runoff), weak upwelling
Arabian Sea: historically fewer cyclones — stronger wind shear, cooler upwelling along Somali coast, drier air
Recent reversal trend: Arabian Sea intensifying faster, reaching higher categories — linked to positive IOD and reduced wind shear
UPSC trap: Cyclone Tauktae (2021) and Biparjoy (2023) — Arabian Sea anomalies; Amphan (2020) — Bay of Bengal super cyclone

concepts.name: Tropical Cyclone Intensity: Rapid Intensification and Ocean Heat Content
key_dimensions: Rapid intensification (RI): wind speed increase ≥35 mph in 24 hours — linked to warm eddies and deep Ocean Heat Content (OHC)
UPSC trap: Sea Surface Temperature alone insufficient — need DEEP warm water to prevent cold upwelling from weakening storm
Role of low vertical wind shear in allowing organized convection and RI
Climate change link: warming oceans increasing frequency of RI events — policy dimension for IPCC reports

concepts.name: Temperate Cyclones (Extratropical Cyclones): Formation via Polar Front Theory
key_dimensions: Bjerknes Polar Front Theory: cyclone forms at boundary between polar (cold) and tropical (warm) air masses
Stages: stationary front → wave formation → young cyclone (warm + cold fronts) → occlusion → dissipation
UPSC trap: Occlusion stage = cyclone cuts off from warm air supply = begins to weaken (opposite of tropical where landfall weakens)
Western Disturbances as extratropical cyclones originating over Mediterranean — critical for NW India winter rainfall

concepts.name: Fronts in Temperate Cyclones: Warm, Cold, Occluded, and Stationary
key_dimensions: Cold front: steeper gradient, faster-moving, narrow intense precipitation band, cumulonimbus, thunderstorms
Warm front: gentler gradient, slow-moving, widespread stratiform precipitation ahead of front (nimbostratus)
UPSC trap: Cold front weather is MORE violent but SHORTER duration; warm front weather is LESS intense but LONGER duration
Occluded front: cold catches warm — two types (cold occlusion vs. warm occlusion) — exam-worthy distinction

concepts.name: Western Disturbances: Origin, Track, and Impact on Indian Subcontinent
key_dimensions: Origin: extratropical cyclones over Mediterranean Sea, Caspian Sea, or Black Sea — travel eastward embedded in mid-latitude westerlies
Impact: winter and pre-monsoon rainfall in NW India, Pakistan, Afghanistan — critical for Rabi crops (wheat)
UPSC trap: Western Disturbances are NOT monsoon phenomena — they occur during winter (Oct–April) and are extratropical
Interaction with Himalayan orography: forced ascent intensifies precipitation; link to snowfall in J&K, HP, Uttarakhand

concepts.name: Storm Surge: Mechanism, Destructiveness, and Vulnerability of Indian Coasts
key_dimensions: Mechanism: low pressure + onshore winds pile up seawater — can be 3–10 m above normal tide level
UPSC trap: Storm surge, NOT wind, is the LEADING cause of death in tropical cyclones historically
Factors amplifying surge: shallow continental shelf (Bay of Bengal coast), funnel-shaped coastline (Bangladesh), high tide coincidence
Odisha and Bangladesh extreme vulnerability — 1999 Odisha supercyclone, 1970 Bhola cyclone context

concepts.name: Cyclone Dissipation: Landfall, Cold Water Upwelling, and Extratropical Transition
key_dimensions: Landfall weakening: loss of warm ocean moisture source + increased surface friction
Cold water upwelling: storm's own winds churn up cold deep water, cutting off energy — self-limiting mechanism
Extratropical transition (ET): tropical cyclone moves poleward, acquires frontal characteristics, becomes extratropical — can re-intensify
UPSC trap: A landfalling cyclone can still cause catastrophic RAINFALL inland even after wind weakening (e.g., flooding)

concepts.name: Pressure and Wind Patterns: Tropical vs. Temperate Cyclones
key_dimensions: Tropical: near-circular isobars, pressure gradient steepest near centre, winds spiral inward anticlockwise (NH) / clockwise (SH)
Temperate: elongated/elliptical isobars, V-shaped at fronts, pressure gradient less steep, larger spatial extent
UPSC trap: In Southern Hemisphere, cyclonic rotation is CLOCKWISE — reversal of NH pattern due to reversed Coriolis
Gradient wind vs. geostrophic wind: in tight tropical cyclone, centripetal acceleration significant — gradient wind better approximation

concepts.name: Inter-annual Variability: ENSO, IOD, and MJO Influence on Cyclone Activity
key_dimensions: El Niño: suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity (increased wind shear), ENHANCES Central/Eastern Pacific activity; suppresses Bay of Bengal cyclones
La Niña: opposite effect — active Atlantic hurricane seasons, more Bay of Bengal cyclones
UPSC trap: IOD (Indian Ocean Dipole) — positive IOD can suppress Arabian Sea cyclones but modulate Bay of Bengal activity
MJO (Madden-Julian Oscillation): 30–60 day cycle creating active/inactive windows for cyclogenesis — sub-seasonal predictor

concepts.name: Naming of Cyclones: IMD Protocol and Regional Practices
key_dimensions: North Indian Ocean naming: 13-member WMO panel (India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Pakistan, Maldives, Oman, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Yemen) — India contributes names
UPSC trap: Cyclones in North Indian Ocean were NOT named until 2004 — India pioneered the regional naming system
Retirement of names: particularly destructive cyclones are retired (e.g., Katrina, Nargis) — name never reused
Difference: Atlantic names follow alphabetical list; Indian Ocean follows country-rotation list

concepts.name: Climate Change Impacts on Tropical Cyclone Characteristics
key_dimensions: IPCC consensus: fewer but MORE INTENSE cyclones globally; poleward migration of peak intensity zones
Increased rainfall rates (5–10% more per degree of warming) — thermodynamic constraint (Clausius-Clapeyron)
UPSC trap: Global frequency may NOT increase or may decrease — but proportion of Category 4–5 storms is increasing
Slower translation speeds: storms moving slower = more rainfall and flooding over same area (e.g., Harvey 2017)

concepts.name: India's Cyclone Disaster Management Framework
key_dimensions: Institutional: IMD (forecasting), NDMA (policy), NDRF (response), Coast Guard, INCOIS for storm surge modelling
UPSC trap: IMD issues colour-coded warnings (Green/Yellow/Orange/Red) — NOT the same as Saffir-Simpson scale
National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP): World Bank-funded, focuses on Odisha and AP — multi-hazard early warning
Success story: zero-casualty target — Odisha model (1999: 10,000 deaths vs. 2013 Phailin: <50 deaths) — evacuation protocol

concepts.name: Tropical Cyclone Belts and Seasonality: Regional Patterns
key_dimensions: General belt: 5°–20° latitude in both hemispheres — UPSC trap: NOT equatorial, NOT polar
Seasonality: North Atlantic peak August–October; North Indian Ocean — two peaks (pre-monsoon: April–June; post-monsoon: October–December)
UPSC trap: Arabian Sea has MORE cyclones in post-monsoon than pre-monsoon, but Bay of Bengal post-monsoon dominates overall North Indian Ocean statistics
Northwest Pacific: most active basin globally (typhoons), active nearly year-round with peak July–October

concepts.name: Comparison Table: Tropical vs. Temperate Cyclones — Key Differentiators
key_dimensions: Energy source, core temperature, pressure gradient, size, seasonality, location of origin — standard comparison MCQ territory
UPSC trap: Temperate cyclones are LARGER in horizontal extent but have WEAKER pressure gradients than tropical cyclones
Tropical: no fronts, symmetric; Temperate: fronts essential, asymmetric precipitation distribution
Predictability: temperate cyclones more predictable (baroclinic models); tropical cyclone track more predictable than intensity

concepts.name: Anticyclones and Their Role as Contextual Counterparts to Cyclones
key_dimensions: Anticyclones: high pressure, outward-spiralling winds, clockwise NH / anticlockwise SH — exact opposite of cyclone rotation
Types: cold anticyclones (shallow, e.g., Siberian High) vs. warm anticyclones (deep, e.g., subtropical highs/Hadley Cell subsidence)
UPSC trap: Subtropical High (e.g., Pacific High, Bermuda High) steers tropical cyclones — NOT a surface feature of cold origin
Blocking anticyclone: stationary high that deflects cyclone tracks — linked to extreme weather events and heat waves
